title: ATC technology register seed
sources: Public literature (SPE/OnePetro abstracts, JPT, DOE/NETL, EPA, IEA, journals, operator and vendor disclosures, trade press) and the public ADIPEC 2026 exhibitor directory. Paper counts: Semantic Scholar bulk search, exact phrases.

entries.name: Electric submersible pump (ESP), conventional
entries.summary: A multistage centrifugal pump driven by a downhole electric induction motor, powered via a cable from surface. Used for medium-to-very-high liquid rates, including high-water-cut wells, where reliable electric power is available.

operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: Rated 'Poor' for free gas (Belaid et al. 2016, Table 1); conventional stages tolerate ~10–20% gas volume fraction at intake (Hart E&P)
operating_window.viscosity_or_api: Rated 'Poor' for heavy crude (Belaid et al. 2016, Table 1)
operating_window.other: Needs reliable electric power. System energy efficiency 30–70% (IPIECA). Rated 'Very Good' for high water cut (Belaid Table 1).

entries.capex: Indicative, 1999 US$ basis (Lea & Nickens SPE-52157, tabulated in Belaid et al. 2016): installation ~US$105k, plus equipment of pump ~$25k, motor ~$15k, protector ~$4k, gas separator ~$5k, cable ~$50k and tubing ~$80k. A Permian (Concho) ESP cost about US$100k to replace (JPT, 2016).
entries.opex: Across 13 papers from 2000–2009, average reported ESP run life ranged from 10 to 66 months, with a mean of 27 months (OGJ, Vandevier 2010). Maintenance was ~US$225/month on a 1999 basis (Belaid/Lea & Nickens). Each failure needs a rig workover. SLB cites offshore Qatar rig rates of ~US$120k/day and US$3–5M per ESP workover.

evidence.claim: NPV comparison for a high-rate well (1,900 bbl/d, 2,300 m, 7% WC): ESP gave the highest NPV, US$58.3M, against gas lift at US$55.6M and hydraulic pumping at US$53.3M.
evidence.who: Belaid et al., Petroleum-Gas Univ. Ploiesti (Mining Revue, 2016)

evidence.claim: Wafra field, Divided Zone: average ESP run life (mean time to failure) rose from 157 to 370 days over a 4-year failure-analysis programme (1998–2001).
evidence.who: Divided Zone operator authors (conference paper indexed by KFUPM)

evidence.claim: Chevron SACROC: a routine motor-maintenance programme raised average run time of failed (burned-out) ESP motors from 813 days (1988) to 1,404 days (1991).
evidence.who: Chevron U.S.A. / E.S.P. Inc. authors, in OGJ 1992

providers.name: Shaanxi Aerospace Delin Technology Group Co., Ltd.
Tianjin Premier ESP Pumping Systems Co. ,Ltd.

reference_fit.reason: Well suited to high-water-cut, high-rate wells. However, unreliable power, sand, free gas, viscous oil and scarce workover rigs all shorten run life and lengthen downtime. Some lake platforms historically had no electric power (OGJ 1994).

entries.rationale: High capex and rig-dependent failures. It is the strongest high-rate drawdown option, with a well-documented run-life literature.
entries.caveats: Costs are 1999-basis and indicative only; current costs vary hugely with depth, horsepower and cable length. Run-life statistics are defined in different ways (MTBF, run life of failed units, run life of running units), so they are not directly comparable. The Wafra figures come from an indexed abstract, not the full paper.

entries.name: ESP with permanent-magnet motor
entries.summary: An ESP driven by a synchronous permanent-magnet motor (PMM) instead of an induction motor. It gives higher efficiency and power factor, a shorter motor, and a wide speed range. Used to cut power demand and to run in low-rate or high-temperature applications.

operating_window.depth_m: As for conventional ESP (< 15,000 ft TVD typical, IPIECA)
operating_window.rate_bpd: As for ESP. Borets offers PMMs from low speed (100 rpm) to high speed (6,000 rpm), for ESP and PCP drives
operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: As for conventional ESP; depends on gas-handling stages
operating_window.other: Needs a PM-compatible VSD. Novomet says its PMM is about 30% shorter and lighter than an induction motor of the same horsepower.

entries.opex: Field observations show power efficiency 10–30% better than induction-motor ESPs (SPE-189211). Across more than 200 Colombian installations: active power savings up to 10.5% and reactive power savings up to 40%, with power factor near 1 (SPE-204485). No published run-life advantage was found.

evidence.claim: Kaji-Semoga field, Indonesia: PMM-ESPs showed power efficiency improvements of up to 10–30% over induction-motor ESPs. The authors estimate ~US$750,000/yr of avoided power-generation cost.
Quifa and Rubiales fields, Colombia, >200 PMM installations: active power savings up to 10.5% and reactive power savings up to 40% versus induction motors. Not every well saved real power.
Permian multi-well field trials of 500/700-series PMMs: real power savings of 10–25%, and total input power reductions of 20–30% (mostly from power-factor improvement).

reference_fit.reason: Lower kW and kVA demand helps where generation is weak or unreliable. The workover, sand and gas exposure is the same as for any ESP.

entries.rationale: Gives a consistent 10–30% power saving but no proven run-life gain. Capex premium unknown. Evidence is mainly vendor-hosted SPE papers.
entries.caveats: No published capex premium over induction motors was found (null). Halliburton says TrueSync is up to 20% more efficient (press release, E5-level, not used). Savings depend on load matching and on whether real or apparent power is quoted.

entries.name: Rigless / alternatively deployed ESP (cable, wireline, coiled tubing, through-tubing)
entries.summary: ESP systems that can be installed or replaced without a workover rig. Methods include coiled tubing or cable deployment, or retrieving the pump/motor through tubing on wireline or slickline. Used where rigs are costly, scarce or slow to mobilise.

operating_window.depth_m: TransCoil cable-deployed design extends range to ~12,000 ft (~3,660 m), against ~7,000 ft for conventional CT-deployed ESPs. First Khurais install was set at 4,900 ft in 7-in. tubing. AccessESP ran by slickline to 5,900 ft offshore Nigeria.
operating_window.other: Needs a compatible completion/tubing size. A field trial ran in a high-H2S well (Energies 2025).

entries.opex: Deployment took under 24 h against the typical 10–14 days for rig-based methods, with more than 2 years of continuous runtime in a high-H2S trial (Energies 2025). Aramco's first TransCoil install cut installation time by nearly 50%. The baseline is an offshore conventional ESP change-out, which costs US$3–5M (SLB Qatar).

evidence.claim: Rigless cable-deployed ESP in a high-H2S well: deployed by coiled tubing in under 24 h (against 10–14 days with a rig), with more than two years of continuous runtime.
evidence.who: Energies (MDPI) 2025 peer-reviewed paper on Saudi field trial

evidence.claim: Aramco reports its first rigless TransCoil ESP installation (Khurais, Dec 2016) cut installation time by nearly 50% compared with a rig-based job.
AccessESP reports replacing a worn pump in 72 hours by slickline without killing the well, and claims operators typically lower cost per barrel by US$2–5 against conventional ESP deployment.

providers.name: Baker Hughes (TransCoil, with Saudi Aramco; AccessESP)

reference_fit.reason: Directly targets scarce workover rigs and long ESP downtime on platforms. Still needs reliable power and a compatible completion.

entries.rationale: Large intervention-time and cost savings are reported. Capex premium undisclosed. Evidence is one peer-reviewed trial plus operator/vendor reports.
entries.caveats: No capex figures were published (null). The cost/bbl and offshore change-out figures are vendor claims. The MDPI page was blocked to direct fetch, so its figures come from the search abstract. The Baker Hughes AccessESP page URL implies the product now sits with Baker Hughes; check current ownership. SPE-192469 (SLB wireline trials) gave only an abstract.

entries.name: Continuous gas lift
entries.summary: Gas is injected continuously down the annulus through gas-lift valves into the tubing, lightening the fluid column. It is the incumbent method on most Lake Maracaibo wells and suits deviated, sandy, high-rate wells wherever lift gas and compression are available.

operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: Rated 'Very Good' for free gas (Belaid et al. 2016, Table 1)
operating_window.sand_tolerance: Rated 'Very Good' (Belaid et al. 2016, Table 1); sand does not pass through the operating valve
operating_window.deviation: Deviated and crooked holes lift easily; wireline-retrievable mandrels with orienting devices work in highly deviated wells
operating_window.other: Needs a lift-gas supply and compression. No downhole electrical power needed. System efficiency 10–30% (IPIECA). Rated 'Poor' for paraffin and 'Poor–Average' for high water cut (Belaid Table 1).

entries.capex: Indicative, 1999 US$ basis (Lea & Nickens, tabulated in Belaid et al. 2016): installation ~US$239k per well, gas-lift valve ~$2k (3-yr life), mandrel ~$5k (10-yr life), tubing ~$80k. Compression is excluded or not itemised.
entries.opex: On a 1999 basis: maintenance US$3,000–6,000/month, gas injection ~US$0.24/m³, plus wireline at ~US$1,000/day (Belaid/Lea & Nickens). Valves can be retrieved by wireline without pulling tubing. Energy efficiency is low, at 10–30% (IPIECA). No published field statistics on valve run life were found.

evidence.claim: Buzurgan field (Iraq): applying gas lift to a dead, high-water-cut well with falling pressure restored production from 0 to 396.6 STB/d.
Offshore well S-7: a retrofit gas-lift installation added 78.58 STB/d.

reference_fit.reason: The incumbent method, with infrastructure in place. It tolerates sand and deviation and needs no platform power. Efficiency falls as water cut rises and reservoir pressure drops, and paraffin is a known weakness.

entries.rationale: Low per-well downhole cost, but compression is costly and energy efficiency poor. Operating limits are well documented, but few quantified benefit studies were found.
entries.caveats: Capex excludes compression and gas-gathering, which dominate field cost. A 1990s-era Chacín paper (scite) reports ~90% of ~7,000 Lake Maracaibo wells on gas lift; it was not verified from the full text and is not used as a number here. Belaid Table 1 is a qualitative compilation.

entries.name: Gas lift optimisation and allocation (model-based / automated)
entries.summary: Reallocating limited lift gas among wells using well and network models, plus automated injection control and monitoring, so that field oil output is maximised for the gas available. Used in mature gas-lifted fields with constrained compression.

operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: Applies where lift gas or compression is constrained
operating_window.other: Needs well tests, wellhead and injection metering, and controllable chokes or valves. Gains depend on how far the baseline is from optimum.

entries.opex: Maraven's Lake Maracaibo automation logged well variables every 2 minutes and polled monitors every 6 minutes. During compressor-train shortfalls it trimmed low-priority wells to 30% of optimum injection. It targeted up to 20% optimisation of gas-lift injection (OGJ 1994).

evidence.claim: Creole, Lake Maracaibo: a gas-lift optimisation programme on 30 wells raised oil production by 2,050 B/D for an extra 1,920 Mscf/D of injection gas.
evidence.who: Redden, Sherman & Blann (Exxon Production Research), SPE-5150-MS, 1974

evidence.claim: Maraven (PDVSA) automated gas-lift injection control on more than 1,000 offshore Lake Maracaibo wells, expecting +27,000 b/d of oil over 3 years and up to 20% optimisation of gas injection. This was a projection, not a reported outcome.
evidence.who: Maraven S.A. / Texas Electronic Resources authors, OGJ 1994

evidence.claim: Mumbai High (ONGC): an integrated network optimisation model was implemented on 160 of 700+ wells, giving an immediate gain of over 2,000 bopd and a significant drop in lift-gas need. The model indicated a 2–4% field gain.

reference_fit.reason: Directly addresses legacy gas lift with gas shortages, long injection lines and manual chokes. There are Lake Maracaibo precedents (Creole 1974, Maraven 1994), and capex is low compared with changing lift method.

entries.rationale: Low-capex brownfield lever with Maracaibo-specific evidence. Gains are typically single-digit % field-wide, larger where the baseline is poor.
entries.caveats: No capex figures found (null). Evidence is dated (1974, 1994, 2009). Gains depend on how sub-optimal the starting point is: a five-well reallocation study under a 5.5 MMscf/d cap gained only ~0.36% (core.ac.uk), so a field may already be near optimum. The Petroleum Experts listing is based on general knowledge of the GAP product; no URL was opened.

entries.name: Sucker rod (beam) pumping
entries.summary: A surface beam pumping unit drives a reciprocating downhole plunger pump through a sucker-rod string. It is the most common onshore lift method for low-to-moderate rates and works with viscous oil.

operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: 'Medium' free-gas tolerance (Belaid Table 1); typical pump efficiency 70–80%, falling below 40% with gas interference (SPE-190936)
operating_window.viscosity_or_api: Used for viscous oil (e.g., Boscan field, Venezuela, OSTI 372375)
operating_window.sand_tolerance: Rated 'not recommended' for sand problems (Belaid et al. 2016, Table 1)
operating_window.deviation: Limited: rod/tubing wear in deviated wells (no numeric limit found)
operating_window.other: System efficiency 45–60% (IPIECA). Rated 'Very Good' for high water cut (Belaid Table 1). Needs a large surface unit.

entries.capex: Indicative, 1999 US$ basis (Lea & Nickens via Belaid et al. 2016): installation ~US$141k; tubing ~$80k, rods ~$20k, pump ~$6k. EPA Natural Gas STAR (2003) gives beam-lift capital of US$20,000–40,000 for gas-well dewatering.
entries.opex: A Permian sample of ~25,000 rod-pumped wells showed ~0.66 failures/well/yr in total (pump 0.25, rod 0.22, tubing 0.16), and ~15 months average run time between failures at Wasson San Andres (Texas Tech study). Maintenance was ~US$200/month on a 1999 basis.

evidence.claim: NPV comparison for a low-rate well (375 bbl/d, 2,070 m, 60% WC): rod pumping had the lowest cost/NPV ratio, 30%, against ESP at 35%, gas lift at 44% and hydraulic pumping at 62%.
Amoco northern Permian: beam pumping was the most economical method on total system cost up to ~320 BFPD, against ESP.
evidence.who: Amoco authors, Southwestern Petroleum Short Course

providers.name: Shandong Molong Petroleum Machinery Co., Ltd.

reference_fit.reason: Historically common on electrified Lake wells (Bachaquero-2, JPT 1963) and good for low-rate viscous oil onshore. Limited by platform footprint, deviation, sand, gas and high fluid rates.

entries.rationale: Cheap and reliable at low rates, with good failure statistics. Rate ceiling and sand and deviation limits cap the benefit.
entries.caveats: The SWPSC Amoco figure was seen only in a search snippet and the ppdl link may not be the exact paper; treat it as indicative. Tenaris and Lufkin are listed from general industry knowledge, without a URL opened. Cost data are dated.

entries.name: Rod lift automation: pump-off control and dynamometer analytics
entries.summary: Controllers read surface and downhole dynamometer cards to detect pump-off and stop or slow the unit. Analytics, increasingly ML-based, classify card shapes to diagnose failures early. Used to cut fluid pound, rod and pump failures, and energy use on rod-pumped wells.

operating_window.other: Applies to beam/rod-pumped wells. Needs load cell, position sensor, controller and (for supervisory systems) communications.

entries.opex: Amoco study of 671 wells: downhole pump failures fell 20% (495 to 396/yr) and sucker-rod failures fell 5%, but workover frequency rose 31% and power use did not fall. Benefits paid back installation cost in under a year on average.

evidence.claim: Amoco (West Texas/SE New Mexico, 671 wells): supervisory pump-off control gave about +10% fluid production and -20% downhole pump failures, with payback under 1 year.
Stetson Petroleum (East Texas, 15 wells): after replacing time clocks with rod-pump controllers, rod and tubing failures fell 31% and electric costs fell 40% over two years.

reference_fit.reason: Low cost, with quick payback on the rod-pumped onshore subset only. Communications and power reliability limit supervisory systems.

entries.rationale: Cheap, with a <1-year payback and 20–30% failure reductions. Evidence is mostly dated trade-press operator reports.
entries.caveats: No per-well controller cost was found (null). The 40% electricity reduction (Stetson) and the 31% rise in workover frequency (Amoco) conflict, so results vary. The Stetson figures come from a search snippet; the full article is paywalled. Modern ML card-classification papers report accuracy but no field failure-reduction numbers. ChampionX Theta/XSPOC is listed from general knowledge, without a URL opened.

entries.name: Long-stroke rod pumping unit
entries.summary: A rod-lift surface unit, such as the Weatherford Rotaflex belt/chain type or a hydraulic unit, giving very long, slow strokes (~288 in or more). Used for deeper, higher-rate or failure-prone rod wells, and sometimes as an ESP replacement.

operating_window.temperature_C: Surface unit operating range −13°F to 275°F (ambient) (RF800 listing)
operating_window.sand_tolerance: Weatherford reports use in sand-laden wells where ESPs failed
operating_window.other: Max stroke 288 in (7,315 mm). RF800: 30,000 lbf polished-rod load, 250,000 in-lb torque. RF950: 36,000 lbf, 350,000 in-lb (Weatherford store listings).

entries.opex: Weatherford reports run life of 519 days against a prior 178-day average (Argentina horizontal well). In a sand-laden well it reports a 75% reduction in cost of ownership, saving ~US$1.1M in 24 months after replacing a failing ESP. A beam pump still has the lowest energy consumption (Sarmiento et al., SPE).

evidence.claim: Weatherford reports that wells with Rotaflex units in high-water-cut areas produced 126% more oil and 68% more fluid over 2 years than area wells on conventional units (32 initial wells).
Weatherford reports that a Rotaflex unit reached a 519-day run life in an Argentine horizontal well, against a 178-day average for the previous rod pump.

providers.name: Zhaoxin Oil Tools (Chinese belt long-stroke units)

reference_fit.reason: Useful for deeper or sandy onshore rod wells. The tall, heavy surface unit is impractical on lake platforms, and deviated wells still suffer rod wear.

entries.rationale: Credible run-life and opex gains, but almost all quantified evidence comes from the vendor.
entries.caveats: No published capex was found (null). Rate and depth ratings were not found and depend on rod and pump design. The SPE paper by Sarmiento et al. (Colombia) is qualitative in the snippet seen. The Dynapump comparison (+130 BFPD) is from a Yates/SWPSC snippet, not opened.

entries.name: Progressing cavity pump (PCP), elastomer stator
entries.summary: A positive-displacement pump: a helical metal rotor turns inside an elastomer stator, usually driven by rods from a surface drive head, or by an ESP motor (ESPCP). Preferred for viscous and heavy oil, sand-laden fluids and low-to-moderate rates.

operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: 'Average' free-gas tolerance (Belaid Table 1). PDVSA-Intevep notes PCPs handle higher gas void fractions than rod pumps
operating_window.viscosity_or_api: Well suited to heavy/viscous oil (PDVSA-Intevep; IPIECA)
operating_window.other: System efficiency 70–80% rod-driven, 75–85% ES-driven (IPIECA). Elastomer swell and compatibility with aromatics and CO2 limit use.

entries.opex: Run life is highly variable. PCM-designed pumps raised average life in Colombian heavy-oil wells from 212 to 420+ days (SPE-209764). A Middle East operator doubled PCP run lives over 4 years by better selection and operating practice (SPE-206909) (both via JPT 2022). Weatherford reports a 60% power reduction against rod pumps at Teca/Nare, Colombia.

evidence.claim: Middle East: PCP run lives doubled over 4 years by applying PCP fundamentals and pump-selection and operating criteria (SPE-206909). Colombia heavy oil: average pump life rose from 212 to 420+ days (SPE-209764).
SLB reports that average PCP run life in four heavy-oil, high-free-gas wells in Albania rose from 133 to 471 days (+254%) with the KUDU Equalizer PCP; the longest run was 1,010 days.
Weatherford reports that PCPs gave a 60% overall reduction in power consumption in Teca and Nare (Colombia), where high water cut plus sand exceeded the rod-pump envelope.

providers.name: Subtor (Weifang) Rotating Precision Machinery Co., Ltd.

reference_fit.reason: Good for the heavy, viscous, sandy, shallow-to-moderate-depth wells, with low energy use. Rod wear in deviated wells, elastomer temperature and fluid-compatibility limits, and high-rate high-WC wells reduce fit; ESPCP is an option on platforms.

entries.rationale: Low capex and high efficiency. Run life varies widely; evidence mixes JPT summaries with vendor cases.
entries.caveats: No per-well capex figure was found (null). PDVSA-Intevep and vendors say capex is lower than ESP, but this is qualitative. Run-life examples are selected best cases, not field-wide statistics. The core.ac.uk PDVSA-Intevep source was blocked to direct fetch, so it is cited from the search snippet only.

entries.name: Metal-to-metal PCP
entries.summary: A PCP with an all-metal stator, no elastomer. Built for high-temperature (thermal/SAGD/steam) heavy-oil wells and for fluids that destroy elastomers.

operating_window.depth_m: Rod-driven 100–3,500 ft (~30–1,070 m) (IPIECA 2023). Rotoliptic R200 designed for lift up to 1,300 m (ERA)
operating_window.viscosity_or_api: Extremely viscous and heavy oil; Orinoco extra-heavy (SPE-171370-MS)
operating_window.other: System efficiency ~35% (IPIECA). Wears faster than elastomer PCPs (JPT).

entries.opex: JPT notes all-metal PCPs typically wear faster than elastomeric PCPs, reducing efficiency and pump life. Rotoliptic's ERA-funded SAGD demonstrations ran for 300+ days with 15–30% lower energy consumption. No published run-life statistics.

evidence.claim: Rotoliptic R200 all-metal PCP: over 300 days of field demonstrations in two Alberta SAGD operations, with 15–30% reductions in energy consumption reported (ERA project, C$3.63M value).
Petropiar (Huyaparí, Orinoco Belt, Venezuela) applied all-metal PCPs to extra-heavy oil where conditions were beyond the limits of elastomer PCPs. No quantified results were visible.

reference_fit.reason: Only relevant where wells are steamed, hot or elastomer-hostile. The depth limit (~3,500 ft), low efficiency and faster wear make it a niche option for most Maracaibo wells.

entries.rationale: Niche thermal technology. Run-life data are thin, and the main quantified evidence is energy reduction from one agency-funded demo.
entries.caveats: Evidence is thin: no capex or run-life statistics were found. The full texts of SPE-171370-MS and SPE-184207 were not accessible. A PCM claim of >800-day SAGD run life was seen only in an unsourced snippet and was not used.

entries.name: Hydraulic jet pump
entries.summary: High-pressure power fluid (oil or water) pumped from surface goes through a downhole nozzle and throat, and the resulting venturi entrains and lifts well fluids. There are no downhole moving parts, and free pumps can be circulated in and out without a rig.

operating_window.depth_m: Setting depths 500–19,000 ft (~150–5,800 m) in successful applications (JPT 2021). Hydraulic pumps generally < 15,000 ft (IPIECA)
operating_window.rate_bpd: < 100 to 20,000 B/D, up to 35,000 B/D (JPT 2021). IPIECA hydraulic-pump range 25–4,000 bpd
operating_window.temperature_C: up to 500°F (~260°C) with HT elastomers (JPT 2021); IPIECA lists 250°F
operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: 'Average–Good' free-gas tolerance for hydraulic pumping (Belaid Table 1)
operating_window.other: Efficiency 20–35%; power fluid can be two or more times the produced volume (IPIECA). Rated 'Average–Good' for paraffin and corrosion (Belaid Table 1).

entries.capex: Indicative, 1999 US$ basis for hydraulic pumping generally, including surface power-fluid system (Lea & Nickens via Belaid et al. 2016): installation ~US$173k, downhole pump ~$20k, tubing ~$80k.
entries.opex: Maintenance ~US$2,900/month on a 1999 basis (Belaid/Lea & Nickens). Energy efficiency is low (20–35%, IPIECA). The downhole pump can be reverse-circulated to surface for change-out without a rig (SLB). No published run-life statistics were found.

evidence.claim: A dead well in a mature field, loaded up for almost 3 years, was revived by jet pump to 380 B/D (100 BOPD + 280 BWPD), exceeding target (SPE-184218-MS).
Counter-evidence: in an NPV comparison for a low-rate well (375 bbl/d), hydraulic pumping had the worst cost/NPV ratio, 62%, against 30% for rod pumping.

reference_fit.reason: No downhole moving parts, tolerance of deviation and heavy oil, and rigless pump changes suit platforms with limited rigs. It can also be set in gas-lift mandrels (Sertecpet). It needs surface power-fluid pumps and is energy-inefficient.

entries.rationale: Moderate capex and high energy opex. Good brownfield flexibility, but few independent quantified field results.
entries.caveats: Capex is for hydraulic pumping generally (piston and jet), on a 1999 basis. The JPT/TWA operating envelope is a summary article, not a standard. The IPIECA and JPT rate and temperature ranges differ, so both are shown. Little independent data on sand handling.

entries.name: Plunger lift
entries.summary: A free-travelling plunger cycles in the tubing, using the well's own gas energy to lift liquid slugs. Used mainly to deliquify gas wells and high-GLR, low-rate oil wells.

operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: Needs GLR of ~400 scf/bbl per 1,000 ft of depth, and shut-in pressure ~1.5× sales-line pressure (EPA 2003)
operating_window.other: Needs no external energy; relies on reservoir gas.

entries.capex: US$1,500–6,000 per well for facilities and set-up (EPA Natural Gas STAR, 2003), against US$20,000–40,000 for beam lift. BP Midland Farm: ~US$10,000 per well installed.
entries.opex: Annual operating cost ~US$500–1,000, payout ~1 month (EPA 2003 economic comparison).

entries.name: Gas-assisted plunger lift and hybrid gas lift

operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: Uses injected gas from the existing gas-lift system

entries.name: Hybrid ESP plus gas lift (dual system / backup lift)
entries.summary: A completion with both an ESP and gas-lift mandrels, or a Y-tool contingency gas-lift path. Gas lift can assist the ESP (reducing pump load) or keep the well flowing when the ESP or power fails, until a rig is available.

operating_window.gor_or_gas_tolerance: Gas lift injected above the ESP packer (SPE-184215-MS)
operating_window.viscosity_or_api: Applied in a viscous-oil marginal field offshore Vietnam (SPE-184215-MS)
operating_window.other: Needs lift gas at the well and a more complex completion. Switchover by slickline sleeve/plug in Y-tool designs (Bokor, Offshore 2010).

entries.opex: Adding 0.28 MMscfd of gas lift cut ESP differential pressure from ~470 to ~388 psi and power by ~2% (SPE-184215-MS). Gas lift kept wells producing during ESP outages (IPA 2019).

evidence.claim: Lamson JOC, offshore Vietnam (Cuu Long Basin): adding 0.2 MMscfd of gas lift to an ESP well raised liquid rate from 1,340 to ~1,740 stb/d (~+30%), with slightly lower ESP power.
evidence.who: Operator paper SPE-184215-MS (2016), summarised at reservoirvn.blogspot.com

evidence.claim: South Sumatra (IB-00XX): during an ESP failure, the hybrid's gas lift kept the well producing and saved ~5,300 bbl of oil.
evidence.who: Arnold et al., Indonesian Petroleum Association 2019

evidence.claim: SLB reports that backup (dual) ESPs in nine offshore Qatar wells produced >2 MMbbl over 5 years that would otherwise have been deferred waiting for workover rigs (~US$120k/day; US$3–5M per workover). This is the dual-ESP variant of backup lift.

reference_fit.reason: Lake wells already have lift gas and mandrels. An ESP adds high-WC drawdown, while gas-lift backup hedges against power outages and rig scarcity. Completion complexity remains, and an ESP repair still needs a rig.

entries.name: Downhole gas separators and gas handling for pumps
entries.summary: Devices that separate free gas before the pump intake (rotary or vortex separators, rod-pump 'gas anchors') or condition and handle gas in the pump (advanced/multiphase gas-handling stages). Used to prevent gas lock, gas interference and short run life in gassy pumped wells.

operating_window.other: Rod pumps: typical pump efficiency 70–80%, falling below 40% with gas interference (Occidental, SPE-190936).

entries.name: Produced water reinjection (PWRI) / waterflood with produced water
entries.summary: Treated produced water is reinjected into the producing reservoir (pressure maintenance or waterflood) or a disposal zone rather than discharged. It is the default disposal route onshore and is increasingly used offshore where discharge limits tighten.

operating_window.capacity_or_rate: Scales from single wells to field-wide; in the US over 90% of produced water has been managed by injection over the 2007-2017 decade (GWPC/Veil 2020).
operating_window.inlet_conditions: Treated to a project-specific TSS and oil-in-water (OIW) limit set by injectivity studies; example training scenario uses TSS ~10 mg/L and ~10 micron particle target (illustrative only).
operating_window.outlet_quality: Spec is reservoir-specific; JPT design study frames it as the optimum TSS/OIW that keeps injectivity over field life.
operating_window.other: Matrix (radial) injection of produced water tends to show continuous injectivity decline; fracture-regime injection is now often designed in. Reservoir thickness, thermal expansion and TSS were the most influential parameters on injection pressure in a JPT modelling study.

entries.opex: Disposal-well injection US$0.07-1.6/bbl (Scanlon 2014, as cited in a 2023 RSC Environmental Science: Advances paper; US onshore); separately reported US$0.75-1.00/bbl for disposal-well reinjection in 2011 (trade press). Excludes transport (US$0.5-8/bbl per Scanlon 2014).

evidence.claim: Over 90% of US produced water was injected (disposal or EOR) throughout the 10-year period to 2017.
Disposal-well reinjection cost averaged 75 cents to US$1/bbl in 2011; trucking to disposal adds ~US$1/bbl.
evidence.who: Greentech Media (citing an industry report and vendor)

evidence.claim: PWRI in matrix injection regime 'inexorably' leads to continuous injectivity decline; design must set TSS/OIW limits and consider fracturing.

providers.name: HEBEI PROVINCE YANSHAN COUNTY DIANLI PIPE FITTINGS CO., LTD
Hubei Petrokh Machine Manufacturing Co., Ltd

reference_fit.reason: Lake Maracaibo fields already waterflood (lake-water injection since the 1960s) and discharge to the lake is the main environmental liability, so closing the loop by reinjecting produced water directly addresses both volume and discharge risk.

entries.rationale: Uses existing injection infrastructure and low per-bbl cost; benefit is avoided discharge plus pressure support; evidence mainly agency/JPT plus dated cost data.
entries.caveats: No published capex band found for PWRI plants (site-specific: pumps, filtration, wells). Cost figures are US onshore and dated (2011-2014). Produced water is richer in nutrients than lake/sea water and can raise souring risk; incompatible mixing with injection water can cause scale. Injectivity decline and frequent workovers are the typical failure mode; requires solids/oil control upstream.

entries.name: Downhole oil-water separation (DOWS)
entries.summary: A downhole hydrocyclone or gravity separator plus pump(s) separates water in the wellbore and injects it into a deeper or shallower zone, so only oil-rich fluid reaches surface. Used in high water-cut wells with a suitable, isolated injection zone.

operating_window.capacity_or_rate: Field trials reported e.g. 43.1 bopd oil with 448 bwpd to surface in an East Texas well (87% reduction in surface water).
operating_window.inlet_conditions: Requires an injection zone with adequate injectivity and isolation from the producing zone; hydrocyclone- (ESP/rod pump) and gravity-type designs.
operating_window.other: Argonne compiled 59 DOWS trials worldwide; in 29 trials with before/after data surface water fell 14-97% (22 of 29 >75%).

entries.capex: Gravity-type installation reported at C$140,000 in one case, with another gravity-type figure in the US$15,000-25,000 range; ESP-type DOWS roughly 2-3x the cost of a standard pump replacement (Argonne, ~1999-2004 basis).

evidence.claim: All 29 DOE-subsidised trials with pre/post data showed reduced water to surface: 14-97%, 22 of 29 exceeding 75%; oil rose in 19 trials, fell in 12.
East Texas trial over ~16 months: 43.1 bopd and 448 bwpd to surface, an 87% reduction in surface water handling.
DOWS reduce produced water disposal costs (trade summary of Argonne findings).

reference_fit.reason: Attractive for very high water-cut wells and limited surface capacity, but needs isolated injection zones, ESP/rod-lift reliability and stable power, and would inject water near zones that are being waterflooded - a poor match for ageing wells with unreliable power.

entries.rationale: Workover plus specialised downhole equipment; large surface-water reductions in trials, but evidence is ~20 years old, mostly Argonne/DOE, with limited recent field use.
entries.caveats: Evidence base is largely 1995-2004 Argonne/DOE trials; I found no recent commercial deployment statistics or current supplier catalogue, so provider list is historical. Opex not found. Failures historically linked to injection-zone plugging and equipment reliability; not all wells are candidates (casing size, injection zone, water quality).

entries.name: Polymer gel water shut-off / conformance
entries.summary: Crosslinked polymer gels (e.g. polyacrylamide with Cr(III) or organic crosslinkers) are pumped into producers or injectors to block high-permeability channels, fractures or watered-out zones. Used for near-wellbore shutoff and in-depth conformance in mature waterfloods.

operating_window.capacity_or_rate: Kansas Arbuckle jobs ~1,500-4,000 bbl gel per well.
operating_window.inlet_conditions: Best for fracture/high-perm channel or flow-behind-pipe problems confirmed by diagnostics; injector gels guideline of >=3000 ppm polymer (Norman et al.).
operating_window.temperature_C: Chromium-acetate gels widely used in moderate-temperature reservoirs; organically crosslinked systems for higher temperatures (no specific limits captured).
operating_window.other: Maracaibo Basin applications sometimes required a gel-cement combination to improve results.

entries.capex: Kansas Arbuckle (2002, US$): gel cost US$30,000-35,000 for larger (~4,000 bbl) and US$15,000-20,000 for smaller (~1,500 bbl) jobs, plus US$5,000-10,000 rig/acid; ~US$45,000 total for large jobs.
entries.opex: One-off well treatment; no recurring opex beyond reduced water handling (savings not quantified in the source).

evidence.claim: ~100 MARCIT gel jobs in the Kansas Arbuckle since 2000; average jobs paid out in 3.8 months (+/-3,200 bbl/well incremental oil over 6 months at US$22/bbl, US$45k job); three poorest jobs did not pay out.
evidence.who: Kansas Geological Survey / Tertiary Oil Recovery Project (Pancake 2002)

evidence.claim: Kelebija field, Serbia: DSGA polymer-gel water shutoff on 7 wells from 2019 with an 85.7% success rate in wells averaging >90% water cut.
Four selective gel water-shutoff applications in mature Maracaibo Lake Basin wells; success tied to diagnosis and selective placement, some requiring gel-cement.
evidence.who: Rauseo et al. (SPE conference paper, PDVSA-area authors)

reference_fit.reason: Directly documented in Maracaibo Basin wells and suits high-water-cut waterfloods with channelling, though success depends on good diagnostics that ageing wells may lack.

entries.rationale: Low cost per well and fast payout in documented programmes; several refereed and agency sources including Maracaibo cases, though cost data are dated (2002).

entries.name: Relative permeability modifiers (RPM)
entries.summary: Water-soluble polymers adsorb on rock and preferentially reduce water permeability relative to oil, allowing bullhead treatment without zonal isolation. Used where water and oil zones cannot be separated mechanically, and in frac fluids.

operating_window.inlet_conditions: Screening from SPE 126845: moderate water cut (50-95%) favourable; low productivity-index wells are bad candidates.
operating_window.other: Vendor claim (Halliburton WaterWeb): >90% reduction in effective water permeability with little hydrocarbon damage. Not effective for long-term shutoff where crossflow exists between oil and water zones (Seright, SPE 99371). Response may take ~2 months (SPE 102711).

evidence.claim: RPM added to frac stimulation: 122% higher gas and 60% lower water production versus offset wells stimulated without RPM (Natural Buttes).
Post-frac RPM treatment cut water ~60% within 10 days and ~80% within a month (700 to 150 b/d).
Halliburton reports WaterWeb reduces effective water permeability by more than 90% with little or no hydrocarbon damage.

reference_fit.reason: Cheap bullhead option for commingled, multilayer wells without isolation, but crossflow in layered Maracaibo sands and reported modest durability limit the gain.

entries.rationale: Low-cost bullhead chemical; benefits documented mostly in gas/frac contexts and vendor data; peer-reviewed caveats on crossflow and longevity.
entries.caveats: No published capex/opex per treatment found. Field data mostly from gas wells/frac applications; oil-well waterflood results in high-water-cut sandstones are thinner. Scribd-hosted SPE copies were seen only as excerpts. Baker Hughes and SLB listed from general knowledge.

entries.name: Mechanical water shut-off (plugs, straddles, expandable patches)
entries.summary: Bridge plugs, cement retainers, straddle packers and expandable steel patches isolate watered-out perforations or casing leaks, often run through tubing on wireline or coiled tubing. Used when water entry point is identified by production logging.

operating_window.inlet_conditions: Requires identified water-entry interval (PLT) and mechanically sound casing; through-tubing high-expansion and inflatable plugs avoid pulling completions.
operating_window.footprint_or_weight: Rigless deployment on e-line/slickline/CT possible; Coretrax expandable straddle left 3.145 in. post-expansion ID.
operating_window.other: Elastomer selection matters in high-CO2 wells (swelling/embrittlement concerns).

evidence.claim: Weatherford reports a wireline-set high-expansion bridge plug in a 71% water-cut well raised oil from 320 to 2,147 BOPD and eliminated 749 BWPD.
SLB reports real-time CT isolation with high-expansion plugs in a 60% water-cut openhole horizontal well (Saudi Arabia) cut water cut by 50% and added ~1,000 bbl/d oil.
Coretrax reports a rigless e-line expandable straddle patch gave ~31% reduction in unwanted water production.

reference_fit.reason: Well-established, low-tech intervention suited to bottom-water or watered-out lower perforations in ageing wells, deployable rigless from platforms, but useless for channelling behind pipe or near-wellbore coning without cement.

entries.rationale: Rigless jobs are relatively cheap and one-off; large gains when the water zone is discrete, but evidence is almost all vendor case studies.
entries.caveats: No published cost per job found. Evidence is vendor case studies (selection bias). Effectiveness depends on accurate zonal diagnostics and casing integrity; ineffective where water cross-flows behind pipe or cones vertically. Baker Hughes listed from general knowledge.

entries.name: Deoiling hydrocyclones
entries.summary: Static liner hydrocyclones use pressure-driven centrifugal force to separate dispersed oil droplets from produced water; the common primary treatment step offshore and onshore.

operating_window.inlet_conditions: Typical feed 500-2,000 ppm oil with droplets mostly <150 um; requires available pressure (pressure drop typically 1-3 bar).

Typical design values d50 10-15 um, reject 1-3%, pressure drop 1-3 bar.

entries.summary: Uses routine rate, pressure and injection data with fast models such as the capacitance-resistance model (CRM) to map injector-producer connectivity, then reallocates water from poorly connected to well-connected injectors and balances patterns. operating_window.other: Turnaround time: allocation update cut from more than a month to under a week (SLB, CNPC Huoshaoshan case).

evidence.claim: Offshore field (Gulf of Thailand): CRM-producer model redistributed a fixed 20,000 BWPD field injection among injectors; forecast oil gain about +1.3 MMSTB across sub-blocks, and one sub-block injector increase from 2,000 to 3,000 BWPD forecast +90 MSTB.
evidence.who: PTTEP (K. Limchuchua), SPE Digital E&P workshop 2024

entries.summary: Injects water with reduced salinity or adjusted ionic make-up instead of seawater or produced water, changing rock-oil-brine chemistry toward more water-wet conditions and lowering residual oil. Best suited to clay-bearing sandstones, ideally in secondary mode.

operating_window.rock: Sandstone with clay present, more clay better; brackish connate water; polar oil components; secondary mode favoured over tertiary (Chavan et al. 2019).
operating_window.carbonates: Engineered water for carbonates should carry Ca2+/Mg2+ and SO4 2- at temperatures above about 70 C (Chavan et al. 2019).
operating_window.api_viscosity: Little evidence that API or viscosity controls the response (Chavan et al. 2019).

entries.name: Cyclic steam stimulation (CSS, steam soak)
entries.summary: Each well is used in turn as injector and producer: steam is injected for days to weeks, the well soaks, and heated, thinned oil is then produced until rates fall and the cycle repeats. It is the main thermal method on Venezuela's Bolivar Coast.

operating_window.depth: Thermal methods mainly applied shallower than 1,100 m; Bolivar Coast fields 1,000-3,000 ft (Vega Riveros & Barrios, SPE-150283, 2011).
operating_window.api: <20 API in general; 11-15 API on the Bolivar Coast (SPE-150283); Tia Juana 10-15 API (de Haan & van Lookeren 1970).
operating_window.viscosity: >50 cp; Bolivar Coast 100-10,000 cp, northern Tia Juana about 20,000 cp (SPE-150283).
operating_window.net_pay: Bolivar Coast sands 50-300 ft; Tia Juana average net 130 ft (SPE-150283; de Haan 1970).
operating_window.performance: Incremental oil-steam ratio 1.5 to 6.8 for CSS (SPE-150283).
operating_window.other: Well spacing typically 2-5 acres; tubing collapse under steam cycling reported at Tia Juana and Lagunillas (search snippet).

entries.capex: Kern River (1990s basis): producer about US$65,000 at 1,000 ft, injector about US$50,000 (OGJ 1997; shallow California wells).
entries.opex: Steam is one-third to one-half of operating expense and fuel gas about three-quarters of steam cost; Kern River operators reported US$2.74-7.94/BOE in 1995 (OGJ 1997).

evidence.claim: Study of Venezuelan heavy-oil steam projects: CSS was the most common method, with incremental oil-steam ratios of 1.5 to 6.8.
Tia Juana (Shell) large-scale steam soak from 1964: STOIIP 2,750 MMbbl of 10-15 API, 100-10,000 cp oil; estimated ultimate primary recovery 18.1%, which steam soak was intended to raise.
evidence.who: de Haan & van Lookeren, Shell, AIME/SPE 1970

evidence.claim: Santa Fe Energy, Kern River: a reinstated cyclic programme plus infill raised lease output from 1,600 to over 4,000 b/d and cut operating cost from over US$8/bbl to about US$4/bbl, for about US$5 million capex over 5 years.

entries.name: CO2 miscible flooding (CO2 EOR, usually as CO2-WAG)
entries.summary: Injects CO2 above minimum miscibility pressure so that it mixes with the oil, swells it and cuts its viscosity, recovering waterflood residual oil; CO2 is recycled and often alternated with water. It can also store CO2 at the same time.

operating_window.performance: Adds 4-15 points of OOIP over primary plus secondary, pilots up to 22% (NETL). WAG ratios 0.5-4 and total CO2 15-30% HCPV (NETL).

entries.capex: Industry spent more than US$1 billion on 2,200 miles of Permian CO2 pipeline; illustrative capital amortisation US$5-10 per bbl (NETL CO2 EOR Primer, c.2010).
entries.opex: Illustrative: CO2 costs about US$15/bbl (at US$2/Mcf purchase, US$0.70/Mcf recycle) plus well/lease O&M US$10-15/bbl, at US$70/bbl oil; total CO2 costs 25-50% of cost per barrel (NETL Primer, c.2010).

evidence.claim: CO2 EOR has added 4-15 percentage points of OOIP over primary and secondary recovery (typically 30-35%), with some pilots reporting up to 22%.
evidence.who: US DOE NETL, CO2 EOR Primer

evidence.claim: Weyburn (Saskatchewan): CO2 injection from Dakota Gasification is expected to recover 130 million incremental barrels and store about 30 million tonnes of CO2.
evidence.who: US DOE NETL, CO2 EOR Primer

evidence.claim: Next-generation CO2 EOR study for the Permian: incremental recovery averages 14% OOIP under current best practice, rising to 28% with next-generation technology.
evidence.who: DOE/NETL with Advanced Resources International (search snippet)

entries.name: Hydrocarbon gas or immiscible gas injection and WAG
entries.summary: Re-injects produced hydrocarbon gas (or nitrogen) into the reservoir, continuously or alternating with water (WAG), to maintain pressure, displace attic or residual oil and, with enriched gas, achieve miscibility. Also gives a use for associated gas that would otherwise be flared.

operating_window.other: Gas compression needs reliable power or gas-driven compressors; early gas breakthrough is the main operational problem (Christensen et al. 2001).

evidence.claim: Review of about 60 WAG field applications (1957 onward): almost all improved recovery over water injection, typically by 5-10% OIIP.
evidence.who: Christensen, Stenby & Skauge, SPE Reservoir Evaluation & Engineering 2001 (abstract)

evidence.claim: First immiscible WAG pilot in Lake Maracaibo (VLE-305, Lagocinco, 2000): WAG estimated to add 10-12% STOOIP; waterflooding of lake light-oil fields not expected to exceed 30% recovery.

entries.name: Matrix acidizing (carbonate HCl and sandstone HF/mud-acid)
entries.summary: Acid is injected below fracture pressure to dissolve near-wellbore damage (fines, scale, mud) in sandstones or to create wormholes in carbonates. It is the most common low-cost stimulation for damaged mature wells, placed by bullheading or coiled tubing.

operating_window.mineralogy: Feldspar-rich and fines-migration-prone sands (e.g. Bachaquero, Lake Maracaibo) need more conservative HF treatments to avoid secondary precipitation (SPE abstract, snippet)
operating_window.crude_compatibility: Lake Maracaibo crudes found highly incompatible with HCl unless additives used (Teeuw & Manzano, SPE 5301, 1975)
operating_window.payback: Indonesian single-well case: oil 78 to 191 BOPD, payout 22 days (UIR thesis, snippet)
operating_window.deployment: Placed by rig or coiled tubing unit; cost accounting in a Cameroon case counts 'rig or coiled tubing unit charges' (snippet), i.e. no workover rig strictly required

entries.opex: One-off treatment; repeat interval depends on damage recurrence. No US$ per-job figure was captured.

entries.summary: Wax deposition in tubing, rods and flowlines is removed by hot oil or hot water, aromatic or aliphatic solvents, and prevented by continuous or squeezed paraffin inhibitors and crystal modifiers. Programmes aim to cut thermal remediation frequency and downtime.

entries.name: Corrosion inhibitor programmes (continuous and batch)
entries.summary: Film-forming chemical inhibitors are injected continuously at the wellhead or manifold, or batch-treated down tubing and through flowlines, to slow internal CO2/H2S corrosion of carbon steel. entries.name: Cathodic protection for pipelines and platforms (galvanic and impressed current, including retrofits)
entries.summary: Sacrificial (Al, Zn, Mg) anodes or impressed-current anode beds and sleds polarise steel pipelines and jackets to stop external corrosion. On ageing structures, depleted anodes are retrofitted to extend life.

operating_window.environment: Lake Maracaibo is brackish and highly corrosive; physical-chemical corrosion rates there are about three times those seen in seawater (Benedict, Materials Performance 1989)
operating_window.anode_choice: Mg, Zn and Al-Zn-In anodes have been compared in Lake Maracaibo brackish water (de Rincón et al., NACE paper 10398, 2010); results are abstract-only
operating_window.retrofit: Replacing sacrificial anodes on existing structures is considered economically acceptable mainly in shallow water; cost rises sharply in deep water (EP0240757 patent background). One vendor design used 8 impressed-current sleds in place of the 900+ sacrificial anodes otherwise needed for a 160 m North Sea platform life extension (Deepwater Corrosion Services)
operating_window.power: Impressed current needs a reliable DC power supply (rectifier); galvanic anodes need none

entries.capex: Indicative per-installation cost: about US$10,000–30,000 for a new magnesium galvanic CP package including labour (SoCalGas regulatory data-request response, c. 2014–2015 US$). A vendor rule of thumb puts a new CP system below 1% of total pipeline project cost.

evidence.claim: Lake Maracaibo: over 20 years the pipeline network needed more than 110,000 leak clamps, with >2,300 km of abandoned bare pipe the main galvanic-corrosion source; an extensive corrosion-control programme saved more than US$1 billion over 20 years.
evidence.who: R.L. Benedict, Materials Performance vol. 28, May 1989 (NACE)

evidence.claim: FHWA/NACE cost-of-corrosion study: corrosion of US gas and liquid transmission pipelines costs about US$7 billion a year to monitor, replace and maintain, and coatings plus CP are the main external controls.
evidence.who: Koch et al., CC Technologies/NACE for FHWA (FHWA-RD-01-156, 2002)

evidence.claim: Deepwater Corrosion Services reports that 8 impressed-current anode sleds replaced the 900+ sacrificial anodes otherwise needed to give a 1980 North Sea platform (160 m water) a 20-year life extension.

providers.name: Middle East Specialized Cables ( MESC) LLC
Shaanxi Aerospace Delin Technology Group Co., Ltd.

reference_fit.reason: Lake Maracaibo has a 50-year local record of CP for underwater pipelines and platforms, its brackish water corrodes about 3x faster than seawater, and Benedict reports a US$1 billion saving from corrosion control there.

entries.rationale: Low cost relative to the assets protected, galvanic systems need no power, and there is lake-specific evidence of large savings; the quantified evidence is old and largely abstract-level.

entries.name: Non-metallic and composite flowlines (RTP, spoolable GRE, thermoplastic composite pipe)
entries.summary: Spoolable reinforced thermoplastic pipe (RTP), glass-reinforced epoxy (GRE/RTR) line pipe and bonded thermoplastic composite pipe (TCP) replace corroding carbon-steel flowlines. They do not corrode internally or externally and install quickly from reels with few joints.

operating_window.temperature_C: HDPE liner/jacket rated 140°F (60°C) and PE-RT 180°F (82°C); steel-reinforced RTP design temperature 194°F (90°C); RTR/GRE envelope 200°F (93°C) (Saudi Aramco, OGJ 2018). Spoolable GRE runs at 75°C with 25% aromatics in Cooper Basin (NOV Fiberspar case study)
operating_window.pressure: Saudi Aramco: hydrocarbon service up to 6-in. and 2,250 psi at 180°F; 6-in. steel-reinforced RTP to 3,000 psig; 4-in. steel-reinforced RTP rated 3,200 psig (OGJ 2018)
operating_window.sour_service: Aramco test flowline with up to 7% H2S; aromatics tolerance raised to 50% (OGJ 2018)
operating_window.lake_maracaibo_conditions: PDVSA gas-lift injection lines with Shawcor FlexCord anti-buoyant RTP: 1,000–1,400 psi, 28–38°C, 600–4,000 m lines (OGN 2017). Nine experimental flexible lines in the lake had no material-related failures after three years under API 17J/17B (AMPP paper abstract)
operating_window.offshore: Petrobras/Shell JIP: DNV qualified a 6-in. carbon-fibre/PA12 TCP for WAG service to DNV-ST-F119 with a 30-year design life; first pre-salt pilot planned for 2027 (OGJ; Materials Performance 2021)

entries.capex: Relative only: Shawcor reports that PDVSA cut installation time and cost by up to 35% against steel in Lake Maracaibo, and Steelman (Saskatchewan) saved 20% on total installed cost (OGN, 2017). Saudi Aramco found RTP three times more economical than carbon steel in incremental NPV at Khurais, and a dual 4-in. RTP cost less up front than an internally coated 6-in. steel line (OGJ, 2018). No absolute US$/km figure was found.
entries.opex: No corrosion-inhibitor or CP spend for internal/external corrosion; no published opex figure found. Recommended biannual H2S permeation monitoring at joints in sour service (Saudi Aramco, OGJ 2018).

evidence.claim: Saudi Aramco: a 1-km carbon-steel flowline takes about 70 days to build against under 2 days for RTP; about 80% of steel construction work is eliminated; RTP was 3x more economical in incremental NPV at Khurais, where about 400 km of RTP flowlines were planned by end-2017.
evidence.who: Parvez, Asiri, Badghaish, Al-Dossary, Al-Mehlisi (Saudi Aramco), Oil & Gas Journal, 2018

evidence.claim: Shawcor reports that PDVSA chose anti-buoyant RTP for gas-lift injection lines in Lake Maracaibo for corrosion resistance, fitting 16 wells in the first six days and cutting installation time and cost by up to 35% against steel.
Cooper Basin: spoolable GRE line pipe was chosen over RTP because of HDPE softening risk, and it operates at 75°C with 25% aromatic hydrocarbons.
evidence.who: NOV Fiber Glass Systems (vendor case study)

providers.name: NOV Fiber Glass Systems (Fiberspar, Star, Bondstrand)
Yidao New Material Technology Co., Ltd.

reference_fit.reason: PDVSA has already installed anti-buoyant RTP and flexible lines in Lake Maracaibo. Lake temperatures and gas-lift pressures sit inside RTP ratings, and the non-metallic pipe removes the galvanic and external corrosion behind the lake's leak history.

entries.rationale: Installed cost is reported equal to or 20–35% below steel and installation is much faster; it eliminates corrosion opex. Evidence is operator/vendor disclosure, with no refereed lifecycle study captured.

entries.name: In-line inspection (smart pigging, including tethered and robotic tools for unpiggable lines)
entries.summary: Free-swimming MFL, ultrasonic and caliper pigs map wall loss, cracks and dents along a pipeline. Tethered, bidirectional or self-propelled robotic crawlers inspect short, multi-diameter or launcher-less lines that conventional pigs cannot pass.

operating_window.sizing_accuracy: High-resolution MFL: depth sizing ±10% wt at 80% certainty for general metal loss; POD 90% at 0.1t depth for general metal loss, pitting and grooving (ROSEN RoCombo/RoCorr service flyers)
operating_window.limitations: The 80% band excludes the deepest 10% of features (pipeliner.com.au); MFL typically cannot detect pinholes (UKOPA presentation)
operating_window.unpiggable: ROSEN inspected a 1.3 km, 10-in. platform-to-subsea-manifold oil flowline with a tethered bidirectional self-propelled UT tool launched vertically from the platform, with no DSV or ROV needed
operating_window.line_requirements: Free-swimming tools need launchers/receivers, cleaning and sufficient flow; robotic tools avoid this but cover shorter lengths

entries.capex: Service cost: about US$100,000 per ILI run, or about US$35,000 per mile all-in including cleaning for a 15-mile line (RBN Energy, c. 2015 US$). SoCalGas used a rule-of-thumb US$200,000 per smart-tool run in a 2012 regulatory filing.

evidence.claim: US liquids operators inspected about 47,000 miles with ILI tools in 2013, and the trade association links a steep drop in corrosion-caused incidents to this technology.
evidence.who: AOPL/API strategy report, via Pipeline & Gas Journal, 2015

evidence.claim: Energy Transfer states that corrosion-caused pipeline incidents across the industry fell 76% since 1999 as smart-pig use grew.
ROSEN reports a corrosion and crack inspection of a non-piggable 1.3 km 10-in. offshore riser and flowline using a tethered self-propelled UT tool, avoiding a diving support vessel and ROV.

reference_fit.reason: Prioritising repair or replacement across thousands of km of lake lines needs condition data, and tethered/robotic tools suit short platform-to-platform flowlines without launchers, though many small, multiphase and heavily corroded lines will need cleaning or will be unpiggable.

entries.rationale: Moderate per-run cost; strong directional evidence that ILI-driven integrity programmes cut corrosion incidents, though the percentages come from industry/operator sources rather than independent analysis.
entries.caveats: The 47,000 miles, 76% and ROSEN case details are from search snippets of the cited pages. RBN and SoCalGas costs are from search snippets; the cost year for RBN is inferred from the article series, not confirmed. The sizing specs are from ROSEN flyers seen in search results. No independent PHMSA study isolating ILI benefit was found. Halliburton and Eddyfi are listed from general knowledge without captured URLs.

entries.name: Electromagnetic casing and tubing thickness logging (multi-barrier EM / magnetic defectoscope)
entries.summary: Wireline electromagnetic tools (eddy-current, pulsed or time-domain EM, magnetic imaging defectoscope) measure metal thickness of tubing and of outer casings through the tubing, so casing corrosion can be found without pulling the completion.

operating_window.barriers: Baker Hughes Sondex EMD: up to 4 barriers, ≤2 in. total metal thickness, in 2-3/8 to 20 in. pipe (datasheet). Time-domain EM tool quantifies 4 barriers individually and the 5th qualitatively (JPT, July 2022)
operating_window.tool_size: SLB EM Pipe Scanner 2.125 in. OD runs through tubing to evaluate casing below the shoe (brochure)
operating_window.accuracy: EM-derived production-tubing thickness agreed with surface ultrasonic measurement of pulled tubing within ±10% (gas-field comparison paper, snippet). EM logs report circumferentially averaged loss, so a 50% average loss can hide a fully penetrated spot (KFUPM/SPE Middle East 2017)
operating_window.limitations: Outer-casing sensitivity and vertical resolution fall with 4+ barriers; inner-casing eccentring can make outer losses look smaller (SLB paper, snippet)

evidence.claim: Halliburton reports that an EPX EM tool combined with a multifinger imager assessed 9-5/8 in. and 13-3/8 in. casing in one run, judged integrity adequate and avoided a workover, saving about US$25,000 and one day.

Sajaa field (Sharjah) field trial: a magnetic impulse defectoscope measured tubing and casing thickness independently through tubing, with qualitative detection of a fourth barrier, benchmarked against a multifinger caliper.
A time-domain EM measurement quantified metal loss on four barriers individually and inspected a fifth qualitatively.

reference_fit.reason: Rig-free wireline surveys suit old gas-lift wells, where the casing annulus carries lift gas and casing condition is critical, and workover rigs are scarce. Deviated wells and heavy-oil/paraffin deposits may hamper tool passage.

entries.rationale: A wireline survey costs little against a workover; the benefit is better workover targeting, but published quantified savings are few and vendor-sourced.
entries.caveats: Most figures come from search snippets of abstracts or vendor sheets (Sondex EMD, EM Pipe Scanner, KFUPM paper, ±10% comparison, SLB 4-barrier paper). The JPT 2022 article and SPE-182968-MS were abstract-only. The Weatherford case title refers to a saving but the page returned 403, so no figure is used. No per-log cost was found. GOWell/Probe is listed from general knowledge.

entries.name: Well barrier and annular pressure management (SCP monitoring, diagnosis and sealant remediation)
entries.summary: A structured programme to monitor annulus pressures, diagnose sustained casing pressure (SCP) with bleed-down/build-up tests, set maximum allowable wellhead operating pressures (MAWOP) and remediate leaking barriers with resin or pressure-activated sealants, following API RP 90 and ISO 16530.

operating_window.prevalence: US Gulf of Mexico (MMS data, 2004): 6,650 of 14,927 active wells (~45%) reported SCP; 52% of it on production casing; >75% of SCP was below 20% of MIYP (OGJ 2004)
operating_window.MAWOP_rules: Draft API RP 90 MAWOP is the lowest of 75% of inner-tubular collapse, 67% of outer-tubular MIYP (50% for the last pressure-containing casing), 80% of the N+1 outer MIYP (67% if unmonitored), and 90% of the shoe fracture gradient (OGJ 2004)
operating_window.remediation_lab: Epoxy resin at 0.5 PV reached 7.53 MPa breakthrough pressure and cut crack permeability to 0.02 D (Petroleum Science 2024)

entries.capex: MMS estimated about US$650 million to eliminate SCP in all affected Gulf of Mexico wells (2004 estimate, US$; no per-well basis given).

evidence.claim: MMS/API workshop data: about 45% of active GoM wells had SCP and four serious 1980s accidents were attributed to high SCP. The resulting API RP 90 framework allows most SCP wells (>75% below 20% MIYP) to be managed by monitoring and diagnostics rather than remediated.
evidence.who: MMS (D. Howard) and API/OOC workshop data, reported in Oil & Gas Journal, 2004

evidence.claim: Lab sealing tests: epoxy resin sealant reached 7.53 MPa breakthrough pressure and reduced fracture permeability to 0.02 D; a related study reports 5.47 MPa in a 2 mm crack, 3.48 times that of cement.
A 2024 review states that more than 45% (6,650 of 12,927) of Gulf of Mexico wells had SCP problems, confirming the scale of annular-pressure risk in older offshore stock.

reference_fit.reason: Old gas-lift wells use the A-annulus for lift gas, so outer-annulus SCP and casing leaks threaten both barriers and lift efficiency. Monitoring and MAWOP management need no rig and suit a sensitive lake, while remediation is harder to source.

entries.rationale: Monitoring and diagnostics are cheap and regulator-backed; remediation evidence is mostly lab or anecdotal, so quantified production or cost gains are thin.
entries.caveats: The two GoM denominators differ (14,927 in the 2004 OGJ figures; 12,927 in Ibukun et al. 2024) and are reported as published. The 5.47 MPa / 3.48x figure is from a search snippet of a related study. No field success-rate statistics for resin/sealant SCP remediation were found. Seal-Tite and Wild Well are from general knowledge plus the JPT link above; Interwell and Expro are listed from general knowledge without captured URLs. ISO 16530 is named from general knowledge.

entries.name: Computational pipeline monitoring (CPM) leak detection: mass balance, RTTM and negative-pressure-wave
entries.summary: SCADA-based software compares metered inflow and outflow, runs real-time transient hydraulic models, or detects the pressure wave from a rupture to raise leak alarms and estimate location (API RP 1130/1149/1175).

operating_window.sensitivity: Depends on meter and pressure instrumentation; API 1149 gives a conservative theoretical method to estimate it. Larger leaks are found faster (OGJ, leak detection selection)
operating_window.field_performance: KROHNE PipePatrol on a 120 km, 10-in. ethylene line: average detection time 450 s, localisation accuracy 0.04% of length (PTC 2015 abstract)
operating_window.lab_performance: Improved negative-pressure-wave method: 4.76% mean positioning error on a test rig (AIP Advances 2024)
operating_window.limitations: NPW systems are fast and locate well but give more false alarms than statistical systems, and slow leaks attenuate the pressure-drop signal (Atmos; Chinese field study). Multiphase flow and poor metering reduce sensitivity

evidence.claim: PHMSA-commissioned review of 197 hazardous-liquid incidents (2010–2012): CPM/SCADA was the first identifier in about 12% overall; API/AOPL note this rises to 39% of larger-than-average releases.
evidence.who: Kiefner & Associates for PHMSA (Leak Detection Study, 2012), with API/AOPL comments

evidence.claim: KROHNE reports that a combined RTTM + negative-pressure-wave system on a 120 km ethylene pipeline detected test leaks in 450 s on average, located to 0.04%, with no false alarms under transient operation.
Improved negative-pressure-wave signal processing achieved a 4.76% mean leak-location error on a test platform.

reference_fit.reason: It suits metered export and trunk lines from lake flow stations, but most lake flowlines are short, multiphase and poorly metered, and grid outages disrupt SCADA, so sensitivity on individual flowlines will be low.

entries.rationale: Software on existing SCADA is moderate in cost, but the regulator study shows it finds a minority of leaks first; better on large ruptures.
entries.caveats: The Kiefner 12%/39% figures come from search snippets of the PHMSA webinar and comment documents, not the final report tables. KROHNE and AIP figures are abstract-level. No capex or opex figure was found; PHMSA RIA tables were not retrieved. AVEVA, Honeywell and ESI are listed from general knowledge without captured URLs.

entries.summary: A fibre-optic cable laid along or inside a pipeline, or a network of acoustic sensors, picks up the vibration, noise or temperature change from escaping fluid. The system locates small leaks and third-party interference along the route.

evidence.claim: Distributed fibre-optic sensing was installed over 3 km of a new produced-water pipeline and monitored for several weeks, aimed at ~0.25 in. leaks in buried pipe.

entries.summary: A thermoplastic liner is pulled into a cleaned, corroded steel line, either tight-fit (swaged or roll-down) or grooved and vented, isolating the steel from corrosive fluid while the host pipe keeps carrying pressure. It is used most for water-injection and oil flowlines.

operating_window.temperature_C: HDPE-lined 6-in. water-injection lines run at 167–176°F (75–80°C) and 2,100 psi average, with swings from 32°F to >175°F within minutes (La Ventana, OGJ 2001)
operating_window.service: Grooved flangeless HDPE liners trialled for 5 years in sour/corrosive oil flowlines (ADNOC, JPT 2019); first HDPE liner in Khurais oil flowline (Saudi Aramco, 2023)
operating_window.failure_mode: Where a liner was damaged during remedial work, the exposed steel corroded at up to 1.95 mm/y (North Sea, Wood Group Kenny, PTC 2014)
operating_window.requirements: Line must be taken out of service, cleaned and accessed at insertion and termination points; bends limit pull length

entries.capex: A Swagelining PVDF liner study showed a 25% saving (about US$7.6 million) against super duplex for a 10 km × 10-in. line (trade press, study basis, year not stated). The La Ventana licensee reports cost was 'a fraction' of replacement (2001).

evidence.claim: ASTRA Repsol-YPF lined about 5,000 ft of 30-year-old, corrosion-pitted 6-in. water-injection line in La Ventana field, Argentina, restoring it at a fraction of the cost of new pipe.

ADNOC ran a 5-year field-trial programme of grooved, flangeless HDPE liners in carbon-steel oil flowlines after internal-corrosion loss of containment, and reports them as a cost-efficient corrosion mitigation.
North Sea polymer-lined water-injection pipelines: two damaged-liner locations showed exposed-steel corrosion up to 1.95 mm/y, which shows the lining's value and its sensitivity to liner damage.
evidence.who: Tadjiev, Murray, Stewart (Wood Group Kenny), PTC 2014

reference_fit.reason: It suits onshore Bolívar Coast lines and lake water-injection lines with platform access, but most lake leaks are external and galvanic, which a liner does not stop; heavily thinned subsea lines may lack the host strength, and steam-era heavy-oil lines exceed polyethylene temperature limits.

entries.rationale: Cheaper than replacement and removes internal-corrosion opex, but quantified results are sparse and mostly trade/vendor.
entries.caveats: The PVDF 25%/US$7.6 million figure and the Khurais HDPE liner (title only) come from search snippets. The ADNOC JPT page gives no quantified results. Claims of a 40–60% saving against replacement and of a 13-year recovered spool (Subsea 7) were seen in snippets without a traceable page and are not used. United Pipeline Systems, Subsea 7 and Future Pipe are listed from general knowledge.

entries.name: Methane leak detection and repair (LDAR) with optical gas imaging
entries.summary: Periodic site surveys with infrared optical gas imaging (OGI) cameras find fugitive hydrocarbon leaks, which are then repaired and re-checked. It is the regulatory baseline LDAR method in the US and Canada.

operating_window.detection: Modelled OGI detection: over 80% of well-site emissions detectable from 10 m imaging distance; imaging distance is the dominant parameter; detection threshold up to 3-4x lower for wet gas than dry gas (Ravikumar, Wang & Brandt, ES&T 2017)
operating_window.survey_frequency: Typically annual to quarterly; British Columbia regulated sites surveyed 3x/year (Wilde, Tyner & Johnson, ACS ES&T Air 2025)
operating_window.repair_effectiveness: >90% of leaks found in an initial survey were not emitting at re-survey 0.5-2 years later (Ravikumar et al., ERL 2020, 36 Alberta facilities)
operating_window.other: Ground crew must reach each component; finds component-level leaks but is weather and operator dependent.

entries.capex: Survey-service basis, not equipment: EPA OOOOa technical support document assumed ~US$600 per well-site OGI survey by contractor (as quoted by EDF, c.2016 USD).
entries.opex: Modelled OGI LDAR programme cost ~US$1,045/site/yr for annual and ~US$1,723/site/yr for semi-annual surveys, against EPA estimates of US$1,318 and US$2,285 (Ravikumar & Lyon, EDF Appendix D, c.2016 USD). API argued well-site costs were nearly 3x EPA's figure (in-house programmes).

evidence.claim: At 36 Alberta unconventional gas facilities, >90% of leaks found in the first OGI survey were repaired/not emitting at re-survey, but total fugitive emissions fell only 22% because new leaks appeared between surveys.
evidence.who: Ravikumar et al., Environmental Research Letters 2020

evidence.claim: Regulatory data suggest 3x/year OGI LDAR halves detected emissions at fully compliant BC sites, but independent aerial surveys of the same sites found substantially higher emissions, so reported reductions may be overstated.
evidence.who: Wilde, Tyner & Johnson, ACS ES&T Air 2025

evidence.claim: IEA identifies LDAR as the largest, lowest-cost methane abatement opportunity and estimated ~40% of oil and gas methane emissions could be avoided at no net cost (2019 gas prices).

reference_fit.reason: Low-capex, no-power, no-rig survey method suited to ageing lake platforms and onshore sites, and boat access makes platform surveys practical.

entries.rationale: Cheap per site with several peer-reviewed field studies, but realised reductions are moderate (≈22% to ≈50%) because new leaks recur between surveys.
entries.caveats: Ravikumar 2017, Ravikumar 2020 and Wilde 2025 figures come from abstracts/search summaries, not full text. US$600/survey is an EPA assumption quoted by EDF, and a vendor (Rebellion) offered US$250/site, which was not used. Team, Montrose, SGS and Konica Minolta are named from general knowledge without captured URLs. No Venezuela-specific cost data.

entries.name: Continuous site methane monitoring (fixed point-sensor and scanning networks)
entries.summary: Fixed sensors or scanning lasers installed at a site detect methane continuously, and software localises and estimates the emission so crews can respond in hours rather than at the next survey.

operating_window.detection_limit: Single-blind METEC testing of 11 solutions: 90% probability of detection between 3 and 30 kg CH4/h; 6 of 11 below 6 kg/h (Bell et al., ES&T 2023)
operating_window.quantification: For 0.1-1 kg/h releases, mean relative quantification errors ranged from -44% to +586% (Bell et al. 2023)
operating_window.other: Performance is weather dependent; METEC protocol testing typically runs for months (CSU METEC protocol). Needs site power (often solar) and communications.

entries.opex: ARPA-E MONITOR programme target of US$3,000 per wellsite per year for basic functionality (programme target, not a market price; c.2015-2017).

evidence.claim: In single-blind controlled-release tests, 6 of 11 continuous monitoring solutions reached 90% probability of detection below 6 kg CH4/h, but quantification of small releases was poor (-44% to +586% mean error).
evidence.who: Bell, Ilonze, Duggan & Zimmerle (CSU METEC), ES&T 2023

evidence.claim: In 11 of 15 aerial surveys, 0.05-1.66% of well sites produced 50-79% of well-site methane emissions, so rapid detection of intermittent large emitters drives most of the abatement value.

reference_fit.reason: Useful at large lake flow stations and compressor platforms, but sensors need reliable power and comms that the area's unstable grid and security problems make difficult.

entries.rationale: Independent controlled-release evidence is good for detection, weak for quantification, and there is no captured installed-cost source.
entries.caveats: The PMC10100557 link is taken to be Bell et al. 2023 from search results; figures come from abstracts. The US$3,000/yr is an ARPA-E target. A Colorado figure of US$3,500-12,000/site/yr turned up in search but had unclear provenance and was not used. No capex source was captured. Honeywell, LongPath, Project Canary and Kuva are named from general knowledge.

entries.name: Aerial and satellite methane detection (aircraft LiDAR/imaging spectrometers, satellites)
entries.summary: Aircraft, drones and satellites measure methane plumes over many sites quickly, flagging large emitters for ground follow-up and producing measurement-based inventories.

operating_window.aircraft_LiDAR: Bridger Gas Mapping LiDAR: ~2 kg/h at 90% probability of detection over 7,474 Permian facilities (PMC10448715, 2023); high-altitude imaging spectrometer campaign practical sensitivity ~280 kg/h at 50% POD (same paper)
operating_window.satellite: Single-blind test: Sentinel-2/Landsat 8 detected releases down to ~1.4 t/h; GHGSat quantified a 0.20 t/h release within 13% (Sherwin et al., Sci. Rep. 2023). Nine-satellite test: detections as low as 0.03 t/h under test conditions (Sherwin et al., AMT 2024)
operating_window.throughput: Bridger reports ~10 facilities surveyed per flight hour (PTAC Alberta Field Challenge, vendor-reported)
operating_window.other: Cloud cover limits satellite coverage. Water surfaces reduce shortwave-infrared satellite sensitivity (general knowledge, not sourced here).

evidence.claim: Nearly one million aerial site measurements in six US regions gave a weighted methane loss of 2.95% of gas production, about 3x the government inventory, with 0.05-1.66% of well sites producing 50-79% of well-site emissions.
evidence.who: Sherwin et al., Nature 2024 (Kairos Aerospace data)

evidence.claim: In the first single-blind satellite test, teams correctly identified 71% of controlled releases; GHGSat quantified a 0.20 t/h release within 13%.
Aircraft trial over 100+ Permian tank batteries: sites emitting >10 kg/h accounted for 90%±6% of total emissions.

entries.name: Flare gas recovery system (FGRS)
entries.summary: Compressors (often liquid-ring) recover gas routed to the flare header and return it to fuel gas, sales or reinjection, leaving the flare for emergency relief only.

operating_window.scale: Tabriz refinery 630 kg/h and Khangiran gas refinery 25,000 m3/h flare gas recovered (Zadakbar et al., OGST 2008)
operating_window.equipment: Liquid-ring compressors, 3-phase separators, coolers; modular parallel trains (Zadakbar 2008)
operating_window.emission_reduction: Up to 85% (Tabriz) and 70% (Khangiran) reduction in flare-related emissions (Zadakbar 2008)
operating_window.other: Needs a gas outlet (fuel system, sales line or injection). Retains a safety flare.

entries.capex: US$0.7 million (Tabriz, 630 kg/h) and US$1.4 million (Khangiran, 25,000 m3/h) installed, refinery basis, c.2008 USD (Zadakbar et al. 2008).

evidence.claim: Two Iranian refinery FGRS designs: US$0.7M capex with ~20-month payback and up to 85% emission reduction, and US$1.4M with ~4-month payback and up to 70% reduction.
evidence.who: Zadakbar, Vatani & Karimpour, Oil & Gas Science and Technology - Rev. IFP 2008

evidence.claim: Flare gas recovery system on Gullfaks (North Sea) reported saving 23 million m3 of gas per year.
Eldfisk 2/7 S new flare system with gas recovery cut CO2 by 21,000 t/yr and NOx by 5.3 t/yr against 2014.

entries.summary: Gas-bleeding pneumatic level and pressure controllers, actuators and chemical pumps are converted to compressed instrument air or to electric (often solar-powered) devices, removing routine methane venting.

operating_window.electric_solar: Solar (140 W panel) plus battery (100 Ah) packages at off-grid sites; chemical injection pumps are the largest power draw (Carbon Limits 2016)
operating_window.emissions: Instrument-air controllers emit no methane (EPA Natural Gas STAR)
operating_window.other: Retrofit well shut-in of 1-2 days for electric controllers (Carbon Limits 2016)

entries.capex: Instrument air: compressor/dryer package US$20,000-70,000, total project US$50,000-250,000; electric: ~US$4,000 per controller plus valve, US$4,000 control panel, US$500 per solar panel and battery, US$5,000-8,000 installation per well site (Carbon Limits for CATF, 2016 USD). ARA Petroleum (Oman) replaced diesel generators on remote water-supply wells with a hybrid off-grid semi-fixed solar system powering an ESP.
